blocks.text: At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely, a company that helps websites customize user experiences and test out new features. Experts say the incident, which saw data-stealing malicious software silently injected into sites like the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, was exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content.
The Zoom.com homepage loading the malicious JavaScript file from Optimizely. Image: blog.report-uri.com. Click to enlarge.

According to a blog post from the security firm Report URI, on November 16 malicious JavaScript code was served to visitors of 178 organizations through Optimizely’s platform. Report URI researcher Scott Helme wrote that the payload delivered by the malicious Javascript was rebuilt 26 times during the day, dropping a multi-purpose malware kit that could steal payment card data, cookies and screenshots, and swap any cryptocurrency payment addresses for the attacker’s.

Helme noted the affected websites also served exploit code custom made to attack known vulnerabilities in older Apple iPhone and iPad devices. Known by such names as “DarkSword” and “Coruna,” these are zero-click exploit kits that chain together a half-dozen security holes to seize complete control over outdated devices and extract data.

“The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn’t always remain trustworthy,” Helme wrote. “A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.”

Contacted for comment, Optimizely said that on November 16, 2026 it “identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in the Optimizely Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.”

“We acted swiftly to contain the incident and have fully remediated the identified vulnerability,” reads a written statement shared by Optimizely. “These measures included blocking access to the vulnerable path, deploying a fix, removing the injected code from affected projects, ending active sessions, revoking tokens, and resetting access for affected user accounts. We have also implemented additional protections to prevent malicious code from being delivered in Cloudflare. While the incident has been fully remediated, we are working with third-party experts on a comprehensive investigation.”

Many top web properties no longer fully display content unless visitors agree to let often dozens of third parties serve JavaScript, a powerful web scripting language that enables interactive content. JavaScript code is run on the user’s device, and it can read information displayed in the user’s browser and even modify a website’s appearance or content.

One reason JavaScript is so heavily used is that it enables fairly precise browser fingerprinting and other ways of tracking visitors and clicks. According to the 2025 Web Almanac by HTTP Archive, the median homepage loads at least 22 JavaScript files. But as the incident with Optimizely shows, a compromise at a third-party vendor’s website can quickly snowball into a supply chain attack against downstream websites that end up serving visitors tampered and malicious JavaScript files.

Zach Edwards is a researcher at Infoblox and the co-founder of the ad-tracking service DecryptAds. Edwards said Optimizely is a vendor which often collects data outside of consent flows, with their JavaScript snippets being embedded as close to the top of the page as possible to ensure that it’s one of the first things to render, which is important since the product is primarily built for A/B testing.

“So to make the product work as expected, this code is setup to fire immediately on-page load, and not restrict rendering behind a consent dialog box,” he said. “This means that this supply chain attack didn’t require any clicking or consent to trigger — most of the impacted clients would immediately serve up the payload as soon as someone loaded the page, further increasing risks from this type of JavaScript snippet being compromised.”

Websites can minimize the chances that a breach at a third-party content provider spirals into a supply chain attack by taking full advantage of “Content Security Policies” or CSPs, which specify the domain names that are allowed to serve third-party content. But Edwards said most websites — apart from perhaps the largest e-commerce, social media and financial platforms — don’t even bother with CSPs, or else tend to leave them overly permissive for marketing reasons.

“With literally all websites which embed 3rd party JavaScript resources, if you don’t have a content security policy then if any of those partners get compromised, new domains can be injected into your website via JavaScript which won’t be stopped,” he said. “We’re in the age of JavaScript supply chain attacks and yet almost no one is talking about why content security policies were invented and how this is largely the solution for operators, even though it’s not always simple to get it initially deployed.”

How broadly deployed were CSPs at the websites impacted by the Optimizely attack? According to Report URI, 68 of the sites had no CSP at all, while 50 of them had a CSP that still allowed the malware payload and the data theft. The company found only 24 of the affected sites (15 percent) had CSPs that fully blocked the malicious payload.
Image: blog.report-uri.com.

The overall deployment of CSPs across the Web’s busiest sites is somewhat lower — about 10 percent — according to Helme’s site crawler.ninja, which scans the top million websites daily for security issues. Helme said he hopes this incident will encourage more sites to adopt effective CSPs, noting that it could have been far worse: By Report URI’s estimates, the purveyors of this malware attack managed to steal only around $7,500 worth of virtual currency from affected users, as well as an unknown number of payment card records.
Helme said he often compares the current widespread lack of CSPs to the Wild West.

“Organizations are running all this code, but they don’t know what it’s doing,” Helme said in an interview with KrebsOnSecurity. “This is why we keep seeing such large scale breaches in places [where] there are no checks and rules in place on the code we’re running, so this was kind of inevitable. Once an attacker gets to the point of running code on your site, the question is what do they want to do with that and can they write the script to do it. Now with AI that’s not a problem anymore.”

Internet users can control the JavaScript elements allowed to run on webpages by using simple script-blocking plugins like NoScript. But these tools have always only been effective for diehard security and privacy nerds who are willing to put up with sifting through dozens of JavaScript requests on each new website.

Happily, modern ad blocking software can handily block most third-party JavaScript requests. Ten years ago, the standard security advice for end users was to install antivirus and enable a firewall. These days, your ad/script blocker is your firewall. We explored several options and approaches to blocking ads in our August 2026 story, Who’s Tracking You?
Update, Nov. 18, 7:06 a.m.: Optimizely has published a report (PDF) on its initial findings about the attack.

blocks.text: Ever since the Huang/Nvidia scandal erupted, I’ve been thinking about a short post I wrote back in March, under the headline “Jensen Huang Doesn’t Smell Anything”:

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, during an on-stage interview at The Hill
& Valley Forum last week, was asked “What do you see as America’s
unique advantages that other countries don’t have?”

His answer, after taking a moment to think, “America’s unique
advantage that no country could possibly have is President Trump.”

Huang, newly appointed to the aforelinked President’s Council
of Advisors on Science and Technology, seemingly doesn’t smell
the growing stink.

The stink was the historically low (and sinking) popularity to which Trump’s 2.0 presidency had sunk, just one year in. Undeniable to anyone in touch with reality. Huang’s obsequious Trump-fellating answer to that question would have been eye-catching even a year prior, when Trump first rolled back into office with an aggressive agenda and a surplus of political capital from a clear election victory — but it was, frankly, a startling thing to say in March 2026. It makes a lot more sense, though, given what’s come to light in the last 10 days.

If you’re not paying close attention you might think Huang’s was the sort of answer any major tech CEO might have given. But it’s not. That was a really unusual thing for Huang to say, way out of line with how corporate leaders typically approach politics. The typical approach for large publicly held corporations is to avoid partisan politics. Advocate only for policies directly related to the company’s business, and otherwise stay out. The political winds change direction every few years. George Bush senior in 1988 was the last new president elected from the same party as the outgoing incumbent, and he only lasted one term. It makes no sense for a corporation that intends to continue thriving for more than the next few years to closely align itself with one party — unless they believe that party will remain in power for the foreseeable future, à la the FDR/Truman Democrats, who won five consecutive presidential elections from 1932 to 1948 (and seven out of nine through 1968).

One metaphor I use for politics is a football field. Democrats on the left, Republicans on the right. CEOs typically stay as close as they can to the 50-yard line in the middle of the field. That way, when an election puts the other party in power, they don’t have to move — they just need to turn around. That’s how someone like Tim Cook could maintain good relations with the White House from Obama to Trump to Biden back to Trump again. He just stayed close to midfield and turned around after each election.

Remaining as close as possible to political midfield under Trump required unseemly obsequious tribute, unprecedented in modern U.S. history. Million-dollar tickets to his inauguration. That ridiculous gold trophy. Embarrassing stuff. But that’s ultimately a reflection of Trump’s avarice, not the politics of Cook personally or Apple as a company. That was the price to stay on the 50-yard line. Cook has often repeated that his two personal heroes are Martin Luther King Jr. and Bobby Kennedy (senior, to be clear). He keeps portraits of both of them in his office. He never swapped them out for portraits of, say, Ronald Reagan. Apple never changed its internal policies or language regarding racial and LGBT equality. The Apple homepage never stopped celebrating Martin Luther King Jr. Day — even when it coincided with Trump’s second inauguration.

And yet Trump remains so enamored of Cook that he floated his name to succeed Huang at Nvidia. Tim Apple remains the apple of Trump’s eye. Yet Apple had nothing to change or apologize for when Biden came into office, nor will they again if, as now seems likely, Trump is succeeded in 2029 by a Democrat elected to clean up his kakistocratic kleptomaniacal mess. (Presumably Apple will gladly pony up at least another $25 million to restore the East Wing after Trump’s architecturally ungodly ballroom edifice is torn down.) And Apple certainly won’t need lawyers to defend them from charges of corruption and/or breaches of national security. Nvidia, not so much.

This is what we should want: business leaders who endeavor to stay out of partisan politics, not hopelessly enmesh themselves in it. Industry and politics cannot operate in isolation, but they should avoid intertwinement except where necessary. Great companies stand the test of time. That’s not feasible if you hitch your corporate wagon to one party or the other, no matter the political moment. We don’t think of Procter & Gamble, Coca-Cola, or Berkshire Hathaway as being Democratic or Republican companies. You cannot chart their fortunes over time based on which party was in power in any given decade. You may well have strong political opinions that are far from the 50-yard line, on one side or the other. I do. But you shouldn’t look for those opinions to be validated by industry executives, any more than you should look for business and product-design decisions to be made by elected government officials. True American values put country over party when it comes to business. And, as Calvin Coolidge aptly put it, “The chief business of the American people is business.”

America does possess unique advantages that other countries don’t have. Personal liberties enshrined in our Bill of Rights. A vibrant, diverse, ever-changing melting pot of a citizenry. A strong tradition of the rule of law, placing no man above it. Competitive markets that allow new entrants to supplant entrenched incumbents. Any CEO worth their salt should have an answer to the question of America’s unique advantages that holds true no matter who, from which party, is currently president. And they should believe it.

What makes Huang’s answer so off-putting isn’t that it was so abjectly partisan — politically tone-deaf to the inevitability of Democrats coming back into power, and perversely obsequious to Trump personally — but that Donald Trump is the antithesis to the entire above list of things that actually give America unique advantages other countries don’t have. Trump and the MAGA movement are also decidedly American and uniquely so, but they represent what’s worst about America.
But I give Huang credit for honesty. Clearly, he believed what he said. Huang didn’t just stray from the 50-yard line — he broke for Trump’s end zone.

Jensen Huang on X: "Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I've never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me.

I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. NVIDIA has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. I love our country, and I love NVIDIA.

I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation. 

Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.

Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours.

Jensen"

blocks.text: Since 2010, I've written an annual "year-in-review" blog post0. It has been nearly two years since I quit my job and went into the FIRE, so what has life been like and have I achieved everything I dreamt of?

Life has been pretty chill! I've been reasonably relaxed, seen loads of shows and gigs, travelled around the world a bit, hung out with cool people, and had no major issues with… well, anything. I've got back into using FourSquare / Swarm to track the places I've been to - that's rather fun.
I've ticked off a lot of things I wanted to do - including some interesting new dining experiences.

I haven't done everything I wanted though. My good friend Jessica introduced me to the concept of New Year's Bingo Boards. Twenty-five things that you want to accomplish over the year. I made it 12 completed and two half-completed. That's not bad - but I must do better.
OKR, KPI, O4Q
How did I do against last year's goals? I'm not so into the "quantified self" - all I really record is the beers I drink and the number of steps I take. But let's look a bit more high-level.

Bits and pieces of work.
							
								Yup! A handful of clients, and 
									I landed a grant. I'm not doing brilliantly at being retired 🤣 but it keeps me out of mischief.

Attend - but don't speak - at conferences.
							
								Yup! Went to a whole bunch of conferences and just enjoyed myself. They're a lot more fun when you're not panicking about a talk!

More health - more exercise.
							
								Keeping to a respectable weight. Taking care of some health issues - oh the joys of getting old(er)! - and trying to prevent more.

Travelling.
							
								An epic 
									two-month Interrail trip, plus a week at the 
									Edinburgh Fringe, plus a few other trips. Exhausting but fun!

Shows and Gigs
							
								A dozen plays, half a dozen gigs, then all the shows at Edinburgh. Oh, and I've started reviewing shows for a new website. Culture is pretty great, innit?

Keep blogging.
							
								Hey, you're reading this, aren't you? I now tend to blog every other day unless there's a burning issue I can't wait to write about.

See more friends in person.
							
								Smashed it out of the park, mate! Saw loads of people. 100% recommend chatting shit with your buddies.
On To The Next Year
Do I need to set goals for myself? Without any external motivation, I find it a bit too easy to drift. I should track what I'm doing, but probably don't need to be all quantified-self about it.
So, here's an attempt at a list. Tune in next year to see how it went!

Finish what I start.
							
								I have a lot of projects on the go. Time to make sure they're done and put away.

Learn to solder.
							
								I went to a 
									terrible
									 soldering class a while ago and it right put me off. I've bought a bunch of stuff, now working up the gumption to learn what I'm doing without burning down the house.

Spend more time with friends.
							
								I hate making plans. It takes effort and it's often very easy to sit on the settee eating crisps. Perhaps I should invite people over to eat crisps?

Document more.
							
								I realise that lots of the smarthome & tech stuff we have only exists in my head. I probably ought to write it all down.

Try some new stuff.
							
								That's a bit vague, innit? What else is out there for me to experiment with?
The 2025-2026 series has gone smoothly, no major plot twists and no-one has been re-cast. What will next year be like? Set a reminder to be back here same blog-time, same blog-channel.
All just a little bit of history repeating
Previously on the Terence Eden adventures…
Today is my birthday - so this is when the new year starts for me. ↩︎
The year 2014 is relegated to a pocket universe and can only be accessed in case of emergency. ↩︎

articles.title: Are vibe-coded games making me a substance dualist?
articles.titleZh: Are vibe-coded games making me a substance dualist?

blocks.text: Seeing vibe-coded videogames lately makes me feel weird. The uncanny valley effect isn't "almost real but not quite" which is the case with AI-generated photos and videos. It's "almost human but not quite". And this is what makes me feel weird. What makes a video game more human?
I'm not religious nor really spiritual, but seeing those AI-generated games in action feels soulless in the most explicit way. As if there is literally an absence of soul?

You feel it when a piece of art, regardless of the technical mastery of the artist, or style, or scale, just assures you it came from someone who, like yourself, has had experiences and emotions. It may be a kid's first drawing or a grand symphony, something in it leaves you doubtless about the presence of the ineffable "soul" or whatever you want to call it.
Funny how even inorganic nature, the landscapes, and rocks, and rivers, can feel the same even though there is nothing human, nothing even cellular behind them.

The rationalist in me can provide a meaningful explanation involving evolutionary traits and pattern recognition. Though one can simply choose to see "the soul", and it's fine, it's just how we name things that we can't quite define but mostly agree upon when we experience it.
I never felt the need to go be all woo-woo when describing stuff produced by machines, until I saw vibe-coded videogames.

This recent video by Second Wind "How to Spot AI Art in Games" talks about assets (models, textures, etc.). Some people quickly recognize there is something "wrong", and the video explains common sources of that feeling: wrongly baked lighting, inconsistent structures, bugged out skeletons and more. So, obviously, there is a rational explanation: it feels soulless because it's literally wrong, within the ruleset of the simulated world.
But often I see vibe-coded videogames with pretty decent graphics, where I can't point a finger at very obvious faults. Stuff like this first-person shooter Saltline:

I wanted to test Fable 5.2's quality with one-shot prompts without human feedback.

Everything in this game is from scratch: models, sounds, textures. ~$550 at API pricing, ~2.7M output and 445M input tokens, heavily cached. Took 8 hours!
Play it here: https://t.co/fazOCcyNIH https://t.co/GoCitQ9EVe— Felix Rieseberg (@felixrieseberg) November 9, 2026

Yet it plays and controls and sounds so utterly soulless. I feel like I'm in the Plato's cave looking at high-fidelity shadows on a high-fidelity cave wall, while also knowing that those shadows are cast by real things: people's art used as training data.
Some demoes are presented as impressive, but result in deep dread.

Internal test game created by a single (senior) developer in 5 days using our new tools and engine. Uses WASM mini-engine (ECS, rendering, animations and physics). 100% AI generated assets using our new asset pipeline. Custom character controller. Slop or not? https://t.co/DGSTEIcniH— Sebastian Aaltonen (@SebAaltonen) June 8, 2026
Or this:
There are so many of them.
However, I'm pretty sure:
What I describe is not significant, spiritual, or meaningful; it's just another combo of uncanny valley effects + an expression of sadness and angst about the regress in quality and craftsmanship.
Like CGI in movies, actually good AI-generated visual stuff is not noticeable, so obviously I'm only noticing stuff that's noticeable. (Why CG Sucks (Except It Doesn't))

Small sprinkles of actual, meaningful human attention can change a vibe-coded game completely. At the moment, people who are the loudest about vibe-coding games mostly have bad taste and they seem to actually believe those results look good.
There is no way back.

blocks.text: This week’s version control and forge news, gathered from release feeds for source control clients and forges, the Lobsters vcs tag, Hacker News, and my boosts on Mastodon. Package management news is in the Saturday This Week in Package Management roundup.
Releases

Gerrit 3.15.0 declares Git’s reftable ref storage ready for production after load testing and fixes to the remaining stability and conversion bugs. Administrators can convert a repository between the files and reftable formats from the project screen, as long as the repository receives no writes during the conversion.

A new POST /projects/{project-name}/branches/{branch-id}/commit REST endpoint creates, updates, deletes or renames files on a branch in one commit, with no clone and no change. The caller needs Push access on the branch. An optional base_revision makes the request fail with 409 Conflict if the branch has moved.

Comments and votes can now be marked as AI-generated through an is_ai field, and the UI shows an icon next to them. The aiReview permission moves to a default-deny ACL. An experimental Stack Diff dialog shows the combined diff of a whole relation chain against its base. Gerrit is now built with JDK 25 and Bazel 9, and plugins that declare dependencies in external_plugin_deps.bzl have to move to Bazel modules.

GitButler 0.23.4 narrows its warning for repositories using Git LFS or git-crypt to editing and resolving commits. Auto-merge now works in GitHub repositories that only allow squash or rebase merges. New installs open the native app by default. In that app, a plain git commit on gitbutler/workspace no longer breaks the project, and the app offers to uncommit it and keep the changes.
Also out: Gerrit 3.14.6, 3.13.11 and 3.12.12.
Security
Gitea 28.4.0 lists 21 CVEs, including one in Go’s net/http fixed by building with Go 1.27.4 and two already fixed in earlier 28.x releases. Among them:

CVE-2026-125423: a repository created with auto-init accepted pushes before initialisation had finished. A user allowed to create repositories could push a crafted tree so that writing the README followed a symlink and overwrote a server-side git hook, which ran commands as the Gitea system user.

CVE-2026-123006: since 28.0.0 the dashboard’s repository search returned each repository’s commit status object with the owner’s full user record. Any signed-in user could read the password hash, salt and email address of the owner of any visible repository with a commit status.

CVE-2026-123638: protected file patterns were matched against file names as git prints them. Git quotes names containing a double quote, backslash or control character, so those names matched no pattern and a user with write access could change files under a protected path.

CVE-2026-118535: a repository registered as an owner-level source of scoped workflows kept that registration after a transfer. The new owner could change workflows that still ran in the previous owner’s repositories with their Actions secrets.
CVE-2026-129337: a repository still being created by a migration, fork or template has no server-side hooks, so a user with read access could push to it over HTTP during that window.
CVE-2026-123002: Gitea accepted unlimited wrong TOTP passcodes. Five failures now block further attempts on the account for 15 minutes.
GitHub Desktop 3.6.11 updates its bundled Git to 2.56.1, the release that fixed the six vulnerabilities covered last week.
GitHub

Issue types and issue fields are generally available on repositories owned by personal accounts. Each account can define up to 25 types and 25 fields under Planning in its settings, and both are exposed through the REST and GraphQL APIs and webhooks. Labels and milestones can now also be created from the issue page when a search finds no match.

The dashboard is more compact after feedback that the new default layout showed too little. Pull request and issue lists show six items by default instead of three, long titles stay on one line, and either the Feed or Home tab can be pinned as the default view. The agent sessions section is hidden for accounts with no agent sessions.

Event Streams, in preview behind a waitlist on all plans, lets a client subscribe to a pull request and keep a connection open. GitHub then sends an event when a review is submitted, commits are pushed, a merge conflict appears, a check suite changes status, or the pull request is merged or closed. Events arrive over the connection the client opened, in place of a public webhook endpoint, and the changelog presents it as a replacement for agents polling the API from a laptop.

Secret scanning has a new detector for Cloudflare service tokens, listed as cloudflare_access_service_token. Partner secrets found in public repositories are reported to the issuer, and user secrets raise alerts in public and private repositories.
Elsewhere

Git considers voting to determine its LLM policy (Jonathan Corbet, LWN) reports on a draft voting process that Emily Shaffer posted to the Git list on 21 October. Git’s contribution guidelines have said since October 2025 that anything that looks AI-generated will be rejected. A session at the Git Contributor’s Summit revisited that policy and reached no consensus.

Under the draft, proposals are patches to the project’s documentation and need a second from another eligible voter. Discussion runs for around four weeks, followed by a two-week vote. The draft gives a vote to anyone with a commit merged to next or two code reviews. Patrick Steinhardt suggested a threshold of 25 or 30 commits. The counting method is undecided, and Steinhardt and brian m. carlson both asked for a secret ballot.

Migrating from GitHub to Codeberg (Yorick Peterse) covers moving Inko and a set of personal repositories by hand with Forgejo’s repository migration feature. The GitHub importer stalled for about an hour at rate limits without reporting it, and it does not map users, so assignees had to be set again. GitHub issue types have no Forgejo equivalent and became labels.

CI moved to Forgejo Actions on self-hosted runners, because Codeberg’s shared runners are AMD64 Linux only and time-limited. Peterse reports that a git push typically takes between 5 and 10 seconds, and that a request to raise the Inko organisation’s 1.5 GiB quota was unanswered at the time of writing.

Codeberg reported on the morning of 18 November that codeberg.org was unreachable. The site is unavailable at the time of writing and the issue is ongoing. Codeberg said the domain had not expired or been transferred, but was missing from its registrar account and in clientHold status, and that no email notification had arrived. A follow-up said no warning had arrived under the registrar’s abuse reporting procedures and that a technical issue was the most likely cause.

Stacked diffs with Maiao (kqr, Entropic Thoughts) describes keeping one commit per change on a single dev branch and publishing it to GitHub with the community fork of Maiao. One git review command fetches upstream, rebases the branch, pushes a disposable branch for each commit, and opens a pull request for each as a native GitHub stack. Running it again after amending a commit force-pushes the branches and updates the pull request descriptions and merge targets.

Git Beyond the Basics (Christian Hofstede-Kuhn) is a long tutorial for people who already use add, commit and push, checked against Git 2.56.1. It covers a starting configuration, rerere, the reflog, fixup commits with autosquash, --update-refs for stacked branches, and what worktrees share.

In the signing section’s tests, a plain git rebase or git cherry-pick of a signed commit dropped the signature from the copy, and Forgejo’s “require signed commits” branch protection rejects the result. Passing -S or setting commit.gpgsign signs the new commits. Hofstede-Kuhn’s own signatures come from an OpenPGP smartcard through oct-git in place of GnuPG.
mini.nvim, the library of Neovim modules, now has mirrors on Tangled and Codeberg. Its README lists the GitHub repository as the main one.

rbit is a self-hosted Git forge written in Rust that runs as one binary with SQLite, redb and bare Git repositories in a single data directory. It reads repositories in-process with gitoxide and serves Git over smart HTTP and a built-in SSH server that offers no shell. The feature list covers issues, pull requests, reviews, Git LFS, mirrors, and imports from GitHub and Gitea. Actions jobs run on a separate rbit-runner.

GitHub processed four DMCA notices from Nintendo dated 6 November, IGN reports (Jacqueline Thomas). They target the Switch emulators Yuzu and Citron Neo and firmware for mod chips. Because the firmware’s fork network was larger than 100 repositories, GitHub applied one notice to all 144 repositories in it.

translations: This week’s version control and forge news, gathered from release feeds for source control clients and forges, the Lobsters vcs tag, Hacker News, and my boosts on Mastodon. Package management news is in the Saturday This Week in Package Management roundup.
Releases

Gerrit 3.15.0 declares Git’s reftable ref storage ready for production after load testing and fixes to the remaining stability and conversion bugs. Administrators can convert a repository between the files and reftable formats from the project screen, as long as the repository receives no writes during the conversion.

A new POST /projects/{project-name}/branches/{branch-id}/commit REST endpoint creates, updates, deletes or renames files on a branch in one commit, with no clone and no change. The caller needs Push access on the branch. An optional base_revision makes the request fail with 409 Conflict if the branch has moved.

Comments and votes can now be marked as AI-generated through an is_ai field, and the UI shows an icon next to them. The aiReview permission moves to a default-deny ACL. An experimental Stack Diff dialog shows the combined diff of a whole relation chain against its base. Gerrit is now built with JDK 25 and Bazel 9, and plugins that declare dependencies in external_plugin_deps.bzl have to move to Bazel modules.

GitButler 0.23.4 narrows its warning for repositories using Git LFS or git-crypt to editing and resolving commits. Auto-merge now works in GitHub repositories that only allow squash or rebase merges. New installs open the native app by default. In that app, a plain git commit on gitbutler/workspace no longer breaks the project, and the app offers to uncommit it and keep the changes.
Also out: Gerrit 3.14.6, 3.13.11 and 3.12.12.
Security
Gitea 28.4.0 lists 21 CVEs, including one in Go’s net/http fixed by building with Go 1.27.4 and two already fixed in earlier 28.x releases. Among them:

CVE-2026-125423: a repository created with auto-init accepted pushes before initialisation had finished. A user allowed to create repositories could push a crafted tree so that writing the README followed a symlink and overwrote a server-side git hook, which ran commands as the Gitea system user.

CVE-2026-123006: since 28.0.0 the dashboard’s repository search returned each repository’s commit status object with the owner’s full user record. Any signed-in user could read the password hash, salt and email address of the owner of any visible repository with a commit status.

CVE-2026-123638: protected file patterns were matched against file names as git prints them. Git quotes names containing a double quote, backslash or control character, so those names matched no pattern and a user with write access could change files under a protected path.

CVE-2026-118535: a repository registered as an owner-level source of scoped workflows kept that registration after a transfer. The new owner could change workflows that still ran in the previous owner’s repositories with their Actions secrets.
CVE-2026-129337: a repository still being created by a migration, fork or template has no server-side hooks, so a user with read access could push to it over HTTP during that window.
CVE-2026-123002: Gitea accepted unlimited wrong TOTP passcodes. Five failures now block further attempts on the account for 15 minutes.
GitHub Desktop 3.6.11 updates its bundled Git to 2.56.1, the release that fixed the six vulnerabilities covered last week.
GitHub

Issue types and issue fields are generally available on repositories owned by personal accounts. Each account can define up to 25 types and 25 fields under Planning in its settings, and both are exposed through the REST and GraphQL APIs and webhooks. Labels and milestones can now also be created from the issue page when a search finds no match.

The dashboard is more compact after feedback that the new default layout showed too little. Pull request and issue lists show six items by default instead of three, long titles stay on one line, and either the Feed or Home tab can be pinned as the default view. The agent sessions section is hidden for accounts with no agent sessions.

Event Streams, in preview behind a waitlist on all plans, lets a client subscribe to a pull request and keep a connection open. GitHub then sends an event when a review is submitted, commits are pushed, a merge conflict appears, a check suite changes status, or the pull request is merged or closed. Events arrive over the connection the client opened, in place of a public webhook endpoint, and the changelog presents it as a replacement for agents polling the API from a laptop.

Secret scanning has a new detector for Cloudflare service tokens, listed as cloudflare_access_service_token. Partner secrets found in public repositories are reported to the issuer, and user secrets raise alerts in public and private repositories.

blocks.text: It was 62 years ago, on November 18, 1963, that the push button telephone, or touch tone phone, was first introduced.
Before push button phones

Before touch tone phones, all we had was rotary dialing. The way a rotary phone worked was by rapidly hanging up and picking the phone back up again to create pulses. This was electrically speaking, of course. To dial a four, it did a rapid hang up/ pickup sequence four times. For zero, it did it 10 times.
This also meant larger numbers took more time to dial. Dialing zero took 10 times as long as dialing one.

Touch tone replaced that by superimposing two freqencies between 697 and 941 Hz and 1209 and 1633 Hz to create a 4×4 matrix covering each number. You didn’t have to push the button very long at all for the tone to register. The result was you could dial any number pretty quickly.

Touch tone was a revenue bonanza for the Bell System, which had a monopoly on the telephone market in the United States. They could charge extra for touch tone service as opposed to traditional pulse dialing. And since you didn’t own the phones, but rather leased them, they could charge you more for push button telephones, such as the Western Electric 2500, as well.
Modern cellular phones don’t have buttons, but they still use the same tone frequencies that were introduced in 1963.
Fighting the man

In the late 1970s, my parents had a device on their phones to convert them to touch tone. They just leased the cheaper, older Western Electric rotary phones, and Dad bought a device that replaced the cap on the part of the headset you talked into. It had push buttons and a small speaker in it, and it operated on a AAA battery. When you wanted to dial the phone, you used the keypad in the headset to dial touch tone. It was a little less convenient since you had to change the battery from time to time, but the device probably paid for itself in a matter of months.

These anti-consumer practices led to the 1982 breakup of AT&T into eight companies, with AT&T concentrating on long distance service, and seven regional Baby Bells, which offered local calling. Over time, the Baby Bells were permitted to merge with each other and with other telecommunications companies such as Worldcom. Modern-day AT&T traces its ancestry to Southwestern Bell, while modern-day Verizon traces its ancestry to Bell Atlantic. Yes, Southwestern Bell acquired its former parent company.
Modern versions of the Western Electric 2500

The Western Electric 2500 is no longer produced. But an updated version that looks just like it still exists and you can still buy one. That phone is called the Cortelco 250044. It’s not as heavy or as loud as a vintage Western Electric 2500 because it has updated electronics and a cheaper bell inside, but it has the same vintage look. Used Cortelco 250044s are inexpensive on Ebay. If you want a vintage-looking phone to use with a VOIP service at home, this would be a good choice.
Push button phones and modems

The main reason I concerned myself with tone or pulse dialing was because I had a modem. The ATDT Hayes command instructed a modem like the Commodore 1670 to use tone dialing. ATDP instructed it to use pulse dialing. Tone dialing was faster, so that’s what I used, except for one time I was giving a demo in a building that only had pulse. Hayes modems even had a register you could set to speed up the tone dialing. I used the command AT S11=50 to dial numbers 40 percent faster, which could give you a slight edge when you were fighting busy signals.

David Farquhar is a computer security professional, entrepreneur, and author. He has written professionally about computers since 1991, so he was writing about retro computers when they were still new. He has been working in IT professionally since 1994 and has specialized in vulnerability management since 2013. He holds Security+ and CISSP certifications. Today he blogs five times a week, mostly about retro computers and retro gaming covering the time period from 1975 to 2000.
